text.p: Haile Gebrselassie, the greatest distance runner of his era, took nearly seven seconds off the world 10,000 metres record on Friday, running alone for more than half the race.

The diminutive Ethiopian, who had been preparing to recapture the record from Morocco's Salah Hissou since last October, clocked 26 minutes 31.32 seconds on a warm, still evening at the Bislett Games grand prix.
The mark has now been reduced by almost half a minute since Kenyan Yobes Ondieki broke the 27-minute barrier here for the first time four years ago.
Four pacemakers, the final two of them from Ethiopia, did their job perfectly, pulling Gebrselassie through 4,000 metres nine seconds under world record schedule.
When Habte Jiftar dropped out with 14-1/2 laps still to run, Gebrselassie did not flag, clocking consistent 64 to 65-second lap times as he wove through the lapped runners.
With 1,000 metres left, Gebrselassie was still eight seconds under schedule and running with such confidence and determination that the world record and a $25,000 bonus was a formality.
"Bislett is a wonderful track for long distance running," he said. "If anyone breaks this I will take it back.
"I thought I could have run even faster. Here the air is clean, the oxygen is good and the crowd is great.
"This season I will only run for records, I haven't made my mind up yet about running in the world championships. I will discuss it with my manager."
Earlier, Olympic and world high hurdles champion Allen Johnson repelled a strong European challenge to set a year's best time.
The powerful American, unaffected by four false starts before the runners finally got away, clocked 13.14 seconds, relegating Germany's Olympic bronze medallist Florian Schwarthoff to second place.
Schwarthoff clocked 13.21 with Britain's world silver medallist Tony Jarrett third in 13.30. Jarrett's compatriot Colin Jackson, the world record holder, was fourth 0.04 of a second further back.
Johnson, who said he would race three more times before the Athens world championships in August, praised Schwarthoff's performance.
"We have had a lot of tough races over the years," he said. "It was a tough race, he is very strong."
The German said Johnson had dominated the first half of the race.
"I will try to give him a hard time at the world championships," he said.
Two Commonwealth athletes also set year's bests early in the meeting, first of the Golden Four series.
New Zealander Beatrice Faumunina threw a national record of 68.52 metres in the discus and Australia's Olympic silver medallist Cathy Freeman clocked 49.39 seconds in the women's 400 metres.
"I am relieved," Commonwealth champion Freeman said. "I did not think I was in that shape."
There was a fourth year's best for Romania's Gabriela Szabo, who clocked 14:42.43 in winning the women's 5,000.
